answer:
**Optimize the measured bottleneck before choosing a tool.** A model can be slow because of Python overhead, tiny kernel launches, memory transfers, inefficient operators, oversized computation, or queueing. Compilation, quantization, pruning, and distillation address different causes. [1](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/torch.compiler_troubleshooting.html)

Compilation/export paths can capture graphs and enable fusion or optimized kernels; ONNX Runtime and TensorRT provide execution paths with their own operator, shape, and hardware support. `torch.compile` can reduce overhead but graph breaks or repeated specialization can limit gains. Tool support is version-dependent, so verify the installed stack rather than treating names as guarantees.

Quantization reduces numerical precision and may improve bandwidth/compute efficiency with supported kernels. Structured pruning removes whole channels/blocks that dense hardware can exploit. Distillation trains a smaller model to reproduce useful behavior, potentially changing the architecture and quality tradeoff rather than merely optimizing the same graph.

**Use an incremental experiment.** Establish a warmed-up and cold-start baseline with representative shapes. Apply one change, verify numerical/task quality, then measure end-to-end latency and memory. Include preprocessing, transfers, and postprocessing so an isolated kernel gain is not mistaken for a product gain.

Keep a fallback for unsupported operators or shapes and test tail cases. A smaller model file, fewer FLOPs, or successful export is not proof of lower p99 latency. The final choice should satisfy quality and operational constraints together.

**Technical details and references.**

Profile first: data conversion, CPU dispatch, transfers, kernels, and queueing can dominate different workloads. Compilation/fusion removes Python and intermediate-memory overhead; ONNX Runtime or TensorRT can optimize supported graphs; quantization reduces storage or arithmetic cost when kernels support the chosen dtype. Structured pruning removes channels/heads, while distillation trains a smaller model. [1](https://docs.pytorch.org/docs/stable/torch.compiler_troubleshooting.html) [4](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531) [5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00978)

Validate numerical and task-level parity after each step, including dynamic shapes and unusual inputs. Measure cold start separately from steady-state latency. Compilation can incur guards, graph breaks, and recompilation; compressed weights can still require expensive dequantization. TorchScript is a legacy choice in many current PyTorch paths, so follow the supported export/compiler route for the deployed version. Optimize the measured bottleneck, then rerun end-to-end load tests.
